messages.content: I want to design a typed Rust–JavaScript FFI that preserves Rust’s aliasing guarantees across asynchronous callbacks, cancellation, and garbage collection. What has to be explicit at the boundary for that goal to be meaningful?

The boundary semantics need to say when Rust-owned values can be accessed, what kind of access is permitted, and how long that permission lasts. Those answers must still hold when JavaScript calls back into Rust before an earlier call has finished, when asynchronous work is canceled, and when JavaScript retains a Rust object that may later be collected. A typed interface alone does not establish memory safety if those cross-boundary events leave ownership, borrowing, or object lifetime ambiguous.
Why single out reentrancy? Isn’t a callback just another call through the interface?

It is another call, but it can occur while an earlier call is still active. That matters if the earlier call has access to Rust state and the callback tries to access the same state. The boundary needs semantics that preserve Rust’s rules about conflicting access in that situation; it cannot assume every call has returned before the next one begins. This is a requirement to define the behavior, not a choice of a particular mechanism for enforcing it.
So an asynchronous callback adds a different timing problem?

Yes. An asynchronous callback may run after the call that arranged it has returned. Any permission it has to use Rust state must remain valid under the interface’s lifetime and aliasing rules at the time it actually runs. The design cannot treat a temporary access granted during the arranging call as though it automatically extends to an arbitrarily later callback.
How should I think about cancellation without choosing an implementation yet?

Treat cancellation as a boundary event whose effect on access and lifetime must be specified. In particular, the semantics need to remain safe if cancellation and callback activity interact: cancellation cannot leave a callback able to use Rust storage that has already become invalid, or silently create conflicting access. The goal does not prescribe whether a callback that has started finishes, or how canceled work is represented. It requires an explicit, memory-safe answer rather than an assumption that cancellation makes all outstanding uses disappear.
And JavaScript-retained Rust objects are a separate case from pending callbacks?

They can overlap, but retention raises its own lifetime question. If JavaScript keeps a way to refer to a Rust object after the Rust call that exposed it returns, the interface must define what that reference permits and when the underlying Rust object may be reclaimed. Garbage collection adds another timing dimension: collection and reclamation cannot invalidate an access that is still allowed by the boundary semantics. Conversely, merely being retained by JavaScript should not be taken as an undefined, implicit Rust borrowing rule.
Does preserving Rust aliasing guarantees mean making JavaScript follow Rust’s borrow syntax?

Not necessarily. It means the behavior permitted through the FFI must be compatible with Rust’s aliasing guarantees, even though JavaScript has a different type and lifetime model. The interface’s types are part of expressing the contract, but the contract also has to cover what happens at runtime when calls are reentrant, callbacks are deferred, work is canceled, or JavaScript holds an object. Nothing in the goal selects a particular API shape or enforcement strategy.
Can you put the memory-safety requirement in one place?

Establish memory safety through explicit Rust–JavaScript boundary semantics covering reentrancy, cancellation, and JavaScript-retained Rust objects. Those semantics must preserve Rust aliasing guarantees across asynchronous callbacks, cancellation, and garbage collection. The important point is that the three cases are part of the safety argument, not exceptions left for callers to guess about.
If the interface is safe, is performance just a secondary aspiration?

Performance is also an explicit requirement. Callback latency overhead must be no greater than 20% versus equivalent handwritten unsafe bindings on a declared benchmark suite. The comparison is to equivalent bindings, and it concerns callback latency; it does not by itself specify a particular benchmark workload, measurement method, or result.
What does the ≤20% wording constrain exactly?

It sets a ceiling on callback latency overhead relative to the equivalent handwritten unsafe bindings in the declared benchmark suite. Expressed as a ratio, the latency would need to be at most 1.2 times the comparison latency under the applicable benchmark measurement. The node does not provide the suite or measured latencies, so that is a target, not a claim that the design already meets it.
Why specify handwritten unsafe bindings as the comparison?

They are the stated performance baseline for equivalent callbacks. That makes the target a comparison against bindings written without the proposed typed interface, rather than against an unrelated callback path. Calling the baseline unsafe identifies the kind of binding being compared; it does not say that the baseline is incorrect or that the typed FFI may relax its safety goal to match its speed.
Would it be fair to describe the task as choosing between aliasing safety and the latency target?

No. The goal asks for a typed Rust–JavaScript FFI that preserves Rust aliasing guarantees and establishes memory safety at the boundary, while also achieving the stated callback-latency target. The latency comparison does not qualify the safety requirement, and the safety requirement does not remove the ≤20% target.
I’m trying to avoid a design where each feature looks safe alone but their interaction is unclear.

That is exactly why the boundary semantics have to cover the interactions, not just isolated calls. A callback could be deferred, JavaScript could retain an object it uses, and cancellation or collection could occur while its status matters. The interface needs a coherent account of permitted access and object validity throughout those circumstances. That observation does not determine which representation or implementation to use; it identifies what a memory-safety argument must account for.
Is the benchmark suite already specified by the goal?

No specific cases or measurements are given. The requirement is to achieve ≤20% callback latency overhead versus equivalent handwritten unsafe bindings on a declared benchmark suite. Declaring the suite matters because the comparison needs a stated scope, but the goal itself does not name its contents or report an outcome.
Then the design brief is a typed interface with explicit safety semantics for the difficult lifetime cases, plus a measurable callback-latency ceiling?

Yes. More precisely, it is a typed Rust–JavaScript FFI that preserves Rust aliasing guarantees across asynchronous callbacks, cancellation, and garbage collection. Its boundary semantics must establish memory safety for reentrancy, cancellation, and JavaScript-retained Rust objects. Separately, its callback latency overhead must be ≤20% compared with equivalent handwritten unsafe bindings on a declared benchmark suite.

For the typed Rust–JavaScript FFI, I propose generating typed, generation-tagged handles with fast-path borrow leases, queued reentrant callbacks, cancellation-owned tasks, and GC reclamation after leases end. Can you unpack how those pieces fit together?

The proposal gives each difficult boundary event a way to be represented in the interface. Typed, generation-tagged handles would represent access to Rust objects across the boundary. Borrow leases would delimit access to those objects, with a fast path intended to keep ordinary callback access inexpensive. Queuing reentrant callbacks would keep a callback from immediately running through a boundary state in which access may already be active. Cancellation-owned tasks would give pending asynchronous work an explicit owner when cancellation occurs. Finally, GC reclamation would wait until relevant leases end, so collection does not reclaim an object while permitted access to it is still active. These are proposed mechanisms, not yet a demonstrated safety or performance result.
What work is the type on a handle meant to do, as distinct from its generation tag?

The type conveys what kind of Rust object or operation the handle is meant to represent. The generation tag addresses a different concern: whether a handle still refers to the particular instance for which it was issued. Together, they are meant to make cross-boundary references more constrained than an unqualified reference to Rust storage. The proposal does not specify the handle representation or all the checks needed to make that distinction effective.
So the generation tag is mainly about a JavaScript reference that survives longer than its Rust object?

That is one important case. If JavaScript retains a handle while the object’s lifetime changes, a generation tag can help distinguish an earlier reference from a later use of an identifier that might otherwise look the same. It does not, by itself, settle whether access is currently allowed, whether a borrow conflicts, or when memory can be reclaimed. Those questions still need the lease and lifetime semantics.
What exactly is a borrow lease in this proposal?

Conceptually, it is a bounded permission to access the Rust object through the FFI under the applicable borrowing rules. Its beginning and end matter because the design must know when access is active and when reclamation may proceed. The proposal calls for fast-path borrow leases, but does not specify their representation, their precise acquisition procedure, or the conditions that put an operation on that fast path.
Would the handle itself be the borrow?

It is useful to keep the two roles distinct. A handle can identify the object that JavaScript may ask to access; a lease can express permission for a particular period of access. If merely retaining the handle counted as an unrestricted borrow, JavaScript retention could make the borrowing rule unclear or unbounded. The proposed separation gives the interface a way to discuss an object that remains identifiable without assuming that every possible access to it is continuously permitted.
How does that relate to Rust aliasing guarantees?

The lease semantics would have to prevent access through the FFI from violating Rust’s rules about conflicting uses of the same object. A typed handle identifies the intended object, but identification is not permission to create incompatible access. For the proposal to meet the goal, the boundary must define which leases may coexist, including when callbacks and JavaScript-retained handles are involved. The proposal names the mechanism; it does not yet supply a complete proof of those rules.
Why queue reentrant callbacks rather than just treating them as ordinary callbacks with leases?

A reentrant callback can arrive while an earlier boundary call is still active. Queuing it is the proposed way to avoid immediately executing that callback in the middle of an access that could conflict with it. Leases still matter: when the queued callback does run, its access must be permitted under the borrowing rules. Queuing addresses when execution can begin; it does not replace the need to determine whether that execution may access a particular Rust object.
Does ‘queued’ mean the callback always runs after the outermost Rust call returns?

The proposal does not specify that exact scheduling rule. It says reentrant callbacks are queued, so they are not simply executed immediately at the reentrant point. A full boundary contract would have to state when queued callbacks become eligible to run and how their leases are handled then. It would be premature to infer a specific queue-draining point from the proposal alone.
Could queuing make the safety problem disappear by turning every callback into a later event?

No. It can change the timing of a reentrant callback, but a later callback can still encounter a retained handle, cancellation, or an object nearing reclamation. Its right to access Rust state must be valid when it actually executes. Queuing is one part of the proposed boundary semantics, not a substitute for the handle, lease, task, and reclamation rules.
What does ‘cancellation-owned tasks’ contribute to the asynchronous case?

It makes ownership of pending asynchronous work an explicit part of the proposal. When cancellation occurs, the interface needs an answer for the task and anything it may still use or cause to be called. Tying that work to a cancellation owner is intended to prevent its lifetime from being left implicit. The proposal does not yet say precisely how cancellation is requested, when it takes effect, or whether a callback already in progress completes; those would need explicit semantics consistent with the leases.
Would cancellation automatically end a borrow lease?

That does not follow from the proposal. Cancellation of pending work and the end of a lease are related but distinct events. If access is still active, the interface cannot treat the object as reclaimable merely because cancellation was requested. A safe design would need to define the interaction without assuming that cancellation instantly stops every use of the object.
Suppose JavaScript retains a Rust object while an asynchronous task is pending. Which part of the proposal protects it?

Different parts address different questions. The typed, generation-tagged handle is the proposed cross-boundary reference to the object. A lease governs a period of permitted access. The cancellation-owned task accounts for pending asynchronous work if cancellation occurs. Deferring GC reclamation until leases end addresses active access during collection. Their interaction still needs explicit boundary semantics; no single one of those elements makes all the others unnecessary.
When you say ‘GC reclamation after leases end,’ does that mean garbage collection cannot notice an object until then?

No. The proposal concerns reclamation, not necessarily when a garbage collector notices that an object may be collectible. Its stated constraint is that reclamation follows the end of relevant leases. This distinction matters because collection decisions and the safe point for reclaiming Rust storage need not be treated as the same event. The proposal does not specify the collector’s algorithm or the exact reclamation procedure.
Does waiting for leases also mean a JavaScript-retained handle keeps the Rust object alive forever?

The proposal does not establish that. It distinguishes a retained handle from an active lease and says GC reclamation occurs after leases end. A complete lifetime contract would still have to say how JavaScript retention affects the object’s eligibility for reclamation and what a retained handle permits if the object is no longer available. It would be too much to infer either permanent retention or immediate reclamation from the proposal’s wording.
I want to be careful with the word ‘fast-path.’ Does it claim leases have already been measured as fast?

No. ‘Fast-path borrow leases’ describes an intended form of the proposed mechanism. It is not a measurement. The goal remains callback latency overhead of ≤20% versus equivalent handwritten unsafe bindings on a declared benchmark suite, but the proposal alone provides neither benchmark results nor a declared suite showing that target has been achieved.
Could the queue and lease checks affect that callback-latency comparison?

They are relevant to the comparison because they sit on or around callback execution. The performance requirement would have to be assessed for the proposed FFI against equivalent handwritten unsafe bindings on the declared benchmark suite. No magnitude or direction of their effect is given here, so the proposal should not be described as meeting or missing the ≤20% ceiling.
Can we describe an illustrative interaction without pretending that its exact scheduling policy has been decided?

Yes. Imagine JavaScript holds a typed handle and a Rust call currently has a lease for the corresponding object. If JavaScript invokes a reentrant callback, the proposal says to queue that callback rather than execute it immediately at the reentrant point. If asynchronous work involving the object is canceled, the cancellation-owned task has to account for that work without invalidating active access. If garbage collection also becomes relevant, reclamation waits for leases to end. That illustrates the roles of the mechanisms; it does not specify when the queue drains or exactly how cancellation and collection are implemented.
What is the strongest claim I can make for this proposal right now?

That it proposes a coordinated design: generated typed, generation-tagged handles; fast-path borrow leases; queued reentrant callbacks; cancellation-owned tasks; and GC reclamation after leases end. The mechanisms are aimed at preserving Rust aliasing guarantees across asynchronous callbacks, cancellation, and garbage collection. Establishing memory safety requires their boundary semantics to be made explicit, and satisfying the separate ≤20% callback-latency requirement requires comparison with equivalent handwritten unsafe bindings on a declared benchmark suite. The proposal itself is not evidence that either requirement has already been met.
When may JavaScript reenter, cancel, or collect a handle while Rust holds an active mutable lease?

That is the boundary question the design needs to answer. It helps to separate the events JavaScript may initiate from their effects on the Rust object. A reentrant call must not obtain access that conflicts with the active mutable lease. Cancellation must not make an ongoing use invalid merely because cancellation was requested. Collection of a JavaScript handle must not reclaim Rust storage while the lease still permits access. Those are safety constraints; they do not yet specify exactly when a queued callback runs or when cancellation takes effect.
Does an active mutable lease mean JavaScript must be prevented from calling into Rust at all?

Not necessarily. A call into Rust and access to the leased object are different things. The concern is whether reentry would create access incompatible with the existing mutable lease. The proposal to queue reentrant callbacks offers a way to avoid executing such a callback immediately while the earlier access is active, but the precise rule for handling every possible reentrant call remains to be stated.
So there are two times to consider: when JavaScript attempts reentry and when the callback actually runs?

Yes. JavaScript could attempt a callback while Rust holds the mutable lease, but queuing it would separate that attempt from its execution. The boundary semantics still need to define when execution is allowed and what access the callback can acquire at that time. Moving execution later is useful only if the access is valid when it occurs.
Would the queue automatically make reentry safe?

No. Queuing avoids immediate execution at the reentrant point, but it does not answer how long the mutable lease lasts or whether a queued callback may access the same object once it runs. The safety argument needs both a scheduling rule and a borrowing rule. It also needs to say what happens if the object’s lifetime changes while the callback is waiting.
What if the callback only has a typed, generation-tagged handle?

Holding that handle can identify the intended object, but it does not itself resolve a conflict with an active mutable lease. The question is when the handle may be used to obtain permitted access, not merely when JavaScript may possess it. The generation tag addresses which instance a handle refers to; it does not turn conflicting access into valid access.
Should I interpret ‘while Rust holds an active mutable lease’ as including a callback that tries to borrow through a second handle to the same object?

Yes, that is a useful way to probe the question. Two handles do not necessarily mean two independent Rust objects. If they refer to the object under the active mutable lease, the interface has to preserve the same aliasing constraint regardless of which handle the callback presents. The question is about the underlying permitted access, not just the number of JavaScript references.
What changes for cancellation? JavaScript might request it at any moment, but is the task canceled at that same moment?

Those need not be the same event, and the proposal has not settled their timing. The boundary contract must distinguish a cancellation request from its effect on the cancellation-owned task and any active lease. In particular, requesting cancellation cannot retroactively make Rust’s current mutable access invalid. What the task does next, and when any associated callback ceases to be eligible to run, still require explicit rules.
Is it enough to say that the cancellation-owned task keeps the object alive?

That would be too narrow as a complete answer. Ownership of pending work helps identify who is responsible for its lifetime, but the active mutable lease also has to remain valid until its permitted access ends. The boundary must explain how cancellation and lease termination interact, including cases where cancellation is requested during an operation rather than before it begins. The phrase ‘cancellation-owned task’ alone does not supply that timing rule.
Could cancellation immediately discard a callback that is still queued?

The question leaves that policy open. It is possible to ask whether cancellation affects callbacks that have not started differently from callbacks already executing, but the supplied proposal does not decide either case. Whatever rule is chosen must not leave access rights or object lifetime ambiguous while Rust has the mutable lease.
How about garbage collection: if JavaScript drops its last reference to the handle during the lease, is that already unsafe?

Dropping a JavaScript reference is not itself the same as reclaiming the Rust object. The critical question is whether the active lease continues to protect the Rust access even if the JavaScript handle becomes collectible. The proposal says GC reclamation happens after leases end, so the act of making a handle collectible cannot be treated as permission to reclaim the leased Rust storage immediately.
When I say ‘collect a handle,’ should I distinguish collection of the JavaScript-facing handle from reclamation of the Rust object?

Yes. Otherwise the question conflates two lifetimes. JavaScript may cease retaining a handle, or the garbage collector may determine that a JavaScript-side representation is no longer reachable; neither fact alone states when Rust storage may safely be reclaimed. With an active mutable lease, the proposed reclamation condition is that relevant leases end before GC reclamation of the Rust object.
Does that mean garbage collection itself must wait until the mutable lease ends?

The proposal does not require that wording. It specifies waiting to reclaim after leases end, not preventing the collector from running or noticing an unreachable handle. The important distinction is between GC activity and a reclamation effect that would invalidate Rust’s current access. The boundary semantics need to preserve that distinction when an active lease exists.
If collection is noticed during the lease and the lease later ends, can the object be reclaimed immediately?

The proposal gives a necessary ordering—reclamation after leases end—but does not define every other condition or the exact reclamation time. It would be premature to say that lease termination alone always triggers immediate reclamation. For this question, the key point is that reclamation cannot cut short the active mutable lease.
I see a common issue: JavaScript can initiate an event while Rust is in the middle of an exclusive use, but the event’s effects may need to wait.

That is a helpful distinction. Reentry, cancellation, and collection can each be described by an attempted or observed event and by any later effect on callback execution, task ownership, access rights, or reclamation. An active mutable lease constrains those effects because the interface must not permit incompatible access or invalidate the ongoing Rust use. The exact timing policy for each event is what this question asks the design to make explicit.
Can I give one blanket rule that JavaScript may do nothing to a handle while a mutable lease is active?

That would go beyond what the question establishes and would obscure important differences. Holding or dropping a handle, attempting a callback, requesting cancellation, and reclaiming Rust storage are not the same action. The safety constraint concerns conflicting access and premature invalidation. A complete boundary rule should distinguish which events can be initiated, which effects are deferred, and which accesses are disallowed, rather than treating every JavaScript interaction as identical.
And the opposite blanket rule—that JavaScript may do anything because the lease is a Rust-side matter—would also fail?

Yes. The active mutable lease cannot be invisible to the semantics of cross-boundary access. If a callback uses a retained handle to obtain conflicting access, or if cancellation or reclamation invalidates the Rust object mid-use, Rust’s aliasing or lifetime guarantees would no longer be preserved. The point is not to forbid JavaScript activity as such, but to define its permitted effects while that lease is active.
What would an explicit answer to the reentrancy part have to specify, without choosing it now?

It would need to specify when a callback attempted during an active mutable lease is queued, when queued execution becomes eligible, and how access through its handle is checked when it runs. It also needs to cover whether a callback involving a different object is treated differently from one that would access the leased object. Naming those questions does not assume a particular queue policy or a particular implementation of the lease.
And for cancellation?

It would need to specify what a cancellation request means for a cancellation-owned task while an active lease exists: which work remains capable of executing, how an already active use reaches its end, and when any access associated with the task is no longer permitted. The answer must preserve the current mutable lease’s validity. The proposal does not yet select an exact cancellation point or dictate how callbacks already underway behave.
Finally, what would the GC portion have to settle?

It would need to distinguish JavaScript-side collection of a handle from reclamation of the Rust object, identify how an active lease prevents premature reclamation, and say what happens to a retained handle if the object is no longer available later. The proposed ordering is GC reclamation after leases end. That ordering addresses the active-lease hazard but does not, by itself, specify the entire handle-lifetime contract.
So my question is not simply whether JavaScript is allowed to trigger these events; it is when each can take effect without violating the active mutable lease?

Exactly. The unresolved issue is when JavaScript reentry may execute, when cancellation may change a task’s ability to use the object, and when collection may lead to Rust-object reclamation while Rust holds an active mutable lease. The proposed queue, cancellation-owned tasks, and lease-delayed reclamation frame those questions, but the boundary semantics still need to state the permitted timing and effects explicitly.

I have a hypothesis for the active-mutable-lease question: deferring reentrant callbacks, cancellation drops, and GC reclamation until lease release yields zero alias violations in JSLeaseStress-1. How should I state it without making it sound like an observed result?

State it as a prediction: if those three effects are deferred until the active lease is released, JSLeaseStress-1 will exhibit zero alias violations. The phrase “zero alias violations” is the predicted outcome in that named stress test, not a measurement already obtained and not a general proof of memory safety.
What ties the three deferrals together?

They all address effects that might otherwise overlap an active lease. A reentrant callback could try to access Rust state before the current access ends. A cancellation drop could end the lifetime of something still involved in that access. GC reclamation could invalidate storage while it remains leased. The hypothesis is that postponing those effects until lease release prevents alias violations in JSLeaseStress-1. It does not say that the three effects are identical or that they need identical handling afterward.
Does ‘defer reentrant callbacks’ mean JavaScript cannot attempt to call back while the lease is active?

No. The hypothesis concerns deferring the callback’s execution, not necessarily preventing JavaScript from attempting reentry. An attempted callback can be distinguished from the point at which it is allowed to run. The predicted result depends on avoiding the relevant execution during the active lease; the hypothesis does not specify the full queuing policy.
Why say ‘cancellation drops’ instead of ‘cancellation’?

That wording identifies the effect being deferred. A cancellation request and a drop associated with cancellation need not occur at the same instant. The hypothesis specifically postpones cancellation drops until lease release; it does not claim that JavaScript is unable to request cancellation while a lease is active, nor does it define every consequence of such a request.
If the cancellation request arrives first, would the hypothesis require the task to keep running?

It does not specify that. It predicts an aliasing outcome from deferring cancellation drops while the lease is active. Whether the task proceeds, stops scheduling further work, or has some other response to a request is outside that statement. The important distinction here is that a request must not be conflated with an immediate drop that could affect an ongoing lease.
Is GC reclamation the same thing as collecting the JavaScript handle?

Not necessarily. The hypothesis names GC reclamation as the effect to defer. A garbage collector might identify a JavaScript-side handle as collectible while Rust still holds a lease; the predicted safeguard concerns not reclaiming the relevant Rust storage before lease release. It does not assert that the collector itself must pause or that no JavaScript-side collection activity can occur.
What does ‘until lease release’ mean across all three cases?

Lease release is the proposed timing boundary: while the lease is active, the named effects are held back; after its release, they are no longer held back by that particular lease. The hypothesis does not say that each effect must happen immediately upon release. Nor does it say lease release is the only condition that could matter before a deferred callback executes or an object is reclaimed.
Would it be accurate to say the lease makes a retained handle safe to use at any later time?

No. A lease concerns permitted access during its own lifetime. Deferring reentrant callbacks and reclamation until its release does not grant a retained handle unlimited future access. When a deferred callback eventually runs, the interface would still need valid rules for its access to the object. The hypothesis predicts zero alias violations in JSLeaseStress-1 from the stated deferrals; it does not define every subsequent handle use.
Then what is the precise predicted result?

The precise prediction is zero alias violations in JSLeaseStress-1 when reentrant callbacks, cancellation drops, and GC reclamation are deferred until lease release. It is a prediction about that test under that condition. There is no supplied observation, count from a completed run, or result for other tests.
Can I say the hypothesis establishes memory safety if the test finds zero violations?

That would overstate what the hypothesis and such a test result could establish. Zero observed alias violations in JSLeaseStress-1 would speak to the conditions exercised by that test; it would not by itself establish memory safety for every Rust–JavaScript interaction. At present, even that test outcome remains a hypothesis rather than an observation.
What if I phrase it as ‘deferral prevents all alias violations’?

That drops the important scope restriction. The stated hypothesis predicts zero alias violations in JSLeaseStress-1. It does not assert that every possible execution, callback pattern, cancellation interaction, or garbage-collection event is covered. Keeping the test name in the sentence preserves the actual claim.
Does the hypothesis say that each deferral is individually sufficient?

No. It proposes the three deferrals together: reentrant callbacks, cancellation drops, and GC reclamation are all deferred until lease release. The statement does not isolate their individual effects or predict what would happen if only one or two were deferred.
Could we infer which of the three is most important for the predicted zero?

Not from the hypothesis alone. It identifies a combined condition and a predicted outcome in JSLeaseStress-1, without assigning a share of that outcome to any one deferral. Making a claim about relative importance would require information that is not given here.
How does this bear on the earlier question about what JavaScript may do during an active mutable lease?

It offers a candidate timing rule for certain effects while the lease remains active. JavaScript may attempt reentry or request cancellation, and collection may become relevant, but the hypothesis concerns deferring callback execution, cancellation drops, and GC reclamation until lease release. That is a proposed way to handle the active-lease interval, not a complete statement of everything JavaScript may do or a verified answer to the question.
Suppose a reentrant callback is waiting when the lease is released. Does the hypothesis guarantee it can then execute safely?

No. Release removes the particular active-lease overlap that motivated deferral. A callback’s eventual execution still has to satisfy whatever access and lifetime rules apply at that point. The hypothesis predicts zero alias violations in JSLeaseStress-1 under the stated deferral condition, but it does not specify a universal rule that every queued callback becomes safe to run immediately.
And if a cancellation drop and GC reclamation are both pending at release, does it specify their order?

No. The hypothesis specifies that both are deferred until lease release, not which one occurs first afterward. Any ordering needed to keep later access valid would require explicit boundary semantics beyond this prediction. It would be inaccurate to add a fixed order as though the hypothesis supplied one.
Does ‘zero alias violations’ also imply zero lifetime errors or zero callback failures?

No. It names alias violations specifically. Lifetime errors and callback failures should not be silently folded into that outcome, and the hypothesis does not report findings about them. Deferring reclamation and drops has a clear connection to object lifetime, but the predicted test result is stated only as zero alias violations.
Is there any performance conclusion hidden in this hypothesis?

No. Deferring work could affect when callbacks run, but the hypothesis makes no latency measurement or performance claim. Its predicted outcome is zero alias violations in JSLeaseStress-1 under the three deferrals. It cannot establish the separate callback-latency target.
Give me a concise formulation that keeps the condition, the timing point, and the test scope intact.
Hypothesis: Deferring reentrant callbacks, cancellation drops, and GC reclamation until lease release yields zero alias violations in JSLeaseStress-1.

I want to turn the active-lease question into a plan: specify lease-state transitions for reentry, cancellation, and GC; implement wasm-bindgen handles; then run JSLeaseStress-1 and CallbackBench. What does each part contribute?

Specifying the transitions makes the boundary behavior explicit: what happens to a lease when reentry is attempted, cancellation is requested, or GC becomes relevant. Implementing wasm-bindgen handles puts the proposed cross-boundary handle approach into a concrete interface. Running JSLeaseStress-1 and CallbackBench is the planned evaluation step. None of those runs or their outcomes is being reported here.
What should ‘lease-state transitions’ mean in that first step?

It means describing how the status of permitted access changes as relevant events occur. For each event, the specification should distinguish what can be initiated while a lease is active from any effect that may have to wait until access ends. It should also say what access is allowed afterward. That is a request for explicit rules, not a claim that a particular set of states or transition rules has already been chosen.
Why cover reentry, cancellation, and GC in the same specification?

Because they can all matter while Rust holds an active lease, even though they are different kinds of events. Reentry concerns when another callback may execute and obtain access. Cancellation concerns what happens to pending work and any associated drop. GC concerns when collection may lead to reclamation. Specifying them together helps make their interactions with lease validity explicit rather than leaving each event with an isolated rule that says nothing about the others.
Does specifying the transitions mean deciding that JavaScript cannot initiate any of those events during a mutable lease?

No. The plan is to specify the transitions, not to impose that blanket restriction in advance. An attempted callback, a cancellation request, and GC activity are distinct from executing a callback, dropping something involved in active access, or reclaiming Rust storage. The specification needs to say which effects are permitted at which points while preserving the mutable lease.
How detailed does the reentry part need to be to answer the question?

It needs to distinguish an attempted reentrant callback from its execution and explain how execution relates to an active lease. It also needs to account for access the callback seeks when it does run. The plan does not yet state a particular queue-draining point or claim that merely delaying a callback is sufficient for every access it might make.
What is the corresponding distinction for cancellation?

A cancellation request is not automatically the same as a cancellation-related drop or the end of access. The transition rules should make clear how cancellation interacts with an active lease and with work that may still use the object. The plan calls for specifying that interaction; it does not yet select the exact point at which cancellation takes effect.
And for GC, is the transition about when the collector runs?

The important boundary distinction is between GC activity concerning a handle and reclamation that could invalidate the Rust object. The lease-state specification should say how active access affects the latter. The plan does not require choosing a garbage-collector algorithm or claiming that the collector itself must stop while a lease is active.
Is there a reason to specify these rules before working on the wasm-bindgen handles?

The listed plan puts the lease-state specification first and the wasm-bindgen handle implementation next. That makes the intended boundary behavior something the implementation can express, rather than something inferred solely from the handle representation. It does not imply that the specification is already complete or that the plan prescribes every implementation detail.
